An internal, measurable trait (neuropsychological, cognitive, imaging or physiologic) that lies between genes and a clinical syndrome and may involve fewer genes than the disorder itself.
NIMH research framework, begun in 2009, that studies dimensions of brain and behavioral function across diagnoses; not a clinical diagnostic system.
Cortical blindness with denial of the blindness, usually from bilateral occipital damage.
Optic ataxia, oculomotor apraxia and simultanagnosia, from bilateral parieto-occipital lesions.
Agraphia, acalculia, right-left disorientation and finger agnosia, attributed to the dominant parietal lobe.
Total loss of color perception from a cortical lesion, with the eyes themselves normal.
Loop linking the hippocampus, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus and cingulate cortex, proposed as a circuit for emotion and later tied to memory.
The body map laid out along the primary somatosensory cortex, with hands, face and lips given the most cortex.
The emotional tone, rhythm and stress of speech; its perception and production depend on the right hemisphere.
Sudden, violent, flinging limb movements, classically from a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus.
Memory for facts and events that can be consciously recalled; depends on the medial temporal lobe, including the hippocampus.
Memory for skills and habits shown in performance rather than recall; depends on basal ganglia and dopamine circuits.
Alternating bands of visual cortex driven by one eye or the other; they form during a critical period and need normal input from both eyes.
Movement of newborn neurons from where they are made to their final place in the developing brain; errors can cause heterotopias.
Formation of new neurons after development, notably in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus; its extent in adult humans is debated.
Railroad worker whose 1848 frontal lobe injury from an iron rod changed his personality, a classic case of frontal lobe syndrome.
